name: Letrozole / aromatase inhibitors for height

lead: Aromatase inhibitors such as letrozole block the enzyme that converts androgens into oestrogen. Because oestrogen drives the closing of growth plates in both sexes, researchers have tested these drugs in adolescent boys with short stature or delayed puberty, hoping to slow bone maturation and give more time to grow.

The idea circulates in height-focused communities as a way to 'delay growth plate closure'. Published research relevant to it is limited to paediatric studies, including a registered phase 3 trial of aromatase inhibitors alone and with growth hormone in adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature. No study identified for this article tests the approach in healthy adults.

paras: Aromatase inhibitors reduce oestrogen production. Lower oestrogen slows growth-plate fusion, which in theory leaves a longer window for growth. Letrozole is a nonsteroidal, reversible inhibitor; other agents include anastrozole and the steroidal exemestane. A meta-analysis cited in encyclopedia sources found letrozole safe and effective for improving height and puberty outcomes in children with constitutional delay of growth and puberty.

Reference sources list aromatase inhibitors as causing hot flushes, joint pain and fatigue, with concern for bone density loss and raised cholesterol with long use, and note they are contraindicated in pregnancy and in premenopausal women for their approved indication. They are prescription-only in the US, UK and EU. Sources note slowed bone maturation can be an effect in children; effects of use for height in healthy people are unstudied.

lead: Aromatase inhibitors (AIs) are drugs that block aromatase, the enzyme that converts androgens such as testosterone into oestrogens. Letrozole and anastrozole are reversible nonsteroidal inhibitors, and exemestane is an irreversible steroidal one.[1][2] They are approved mainly for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women.[1][2]

'AI for height' refers to the off-label idea of using these drugs to lower oestrogen in adolescents, slowing growth-plate closure and extending the growing period. Reference sources describe AIs being used experimentally in boys with delayed puberty and idiopathic short stature, where reduced oestrogen slows growth-plate fusion and gives growth hormone more time to work.[2] A meta-analysis of seven randomised trials, summarised in an encyclopedia entry, found letrozole safe and effective for improving height and puberty outcomes in children with constitutional delay of growth and puberty.[1]

A registered phase 3 trial tested aromatase inhibitors alone and combined with growth hormone in 76 adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature.[3] No study identified for this article has tested AIs for height in healthy adults with closed growth plates, and no forum material was identified for this entry.

paras: Letrozole (brand name Femara) is approved for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in postmenopausal women, and is also used off-label for ovulation induction in polycystic ovary syndrome and in some other settings, including constitutional delay of growth and puberty.[1] Aromatase inhibitors are also listed for gynecomastia in adolescents, precocious puberty and short stature in reference summaries.[2]
The World Anti-Doping Agency lists letrozole because it can counter side effects of anabolic steroids; the article notes it does not itself enhance performance.[1]

Growth plates close under the influence of oestrogen in both sexes. Lowering oestrogen with an AI slows bone-age advancement, and it has been tested in boys with delayed puberty or idiopathic short stature, sometimes together with growth hormone.[2][3] An encyclopedia entry on idiopathic short stature mentions AIs only as a proposed alternative to growth hormone.[4]

Common effects of letrozole include sweating, hot flushes, joint pain and fatigue, resembling effects of low oestrogen. Long-term use raises concern about osteoporosis, and precautions cover bone mineral density loss, raised cholesterol and fat levels, dizziness, pregnancy and breastfeeding. It is contraindicated in premenopausal women.[1]

A general reference on aromatase inhibitors lists slowed bone maturation and growth, infertility, aggressive behaviour, adrenal insufficiency, kidney failure, hair loss and liver dysfunction among reported effects, and notes the page says men do not show the same bone effects seen in women.[2]

A phase 3 trial, completed, enrolled 76 adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature to compare aromatase inhibitors alone and in combination with growth hormone.[3] A meta-analysis of seven randomised trials of letrozole in constitutional delay of growth and puberty, cited in an encyclopedia entry, reported improved height and puberty outcomes and slowed bone-age progression.[1] Registered studies of letrozole in congenital adrenal hyperplasia (a three-drug combination) and in ovulation induction concern other indications.[5][6]
No studies found of aromatase inhibitors for height in healthy adults.

Letrozole is prescription-only in the US, UK and EU, and Schedule VII in Canada. India banned its use for ovulation induction in 2011, citing infant safety concerns.[1] It is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1]

timeline.event: Phase 3 trial of aromatase inhibitors alone and with growth hormone in adolescent boys with idiopathic short stature begins.[3]
